title: The Jaundice After the Last Tablet — Delayed Amoxicillin–Clavulanate Cholestatic Jaundice, R-Value Liver Triage, HLA Risk & Beta-Lactamase Acylation

teenKit.tldr: A routine antibiotic can secretly plant a biological time bomb that triggers severe liver damage and yellow skin (jaundice) a full three weeks after you've taken the very last pill.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It shatters our basic intuition that drugs only affect us while they are physically inside our bodies, proving that our immune system can hold a delayed grudge long after a medication is gone.
keyTakeaways: Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury breaks normal rules, showing up weeks after the medication has completely vanished from the bloodstream.
The reaction involves a fascinating drop down in scale from a full human body all the way down to a 1-Angstrom molecular pocket in a bacterial enzyme.
Your own genetics—specifically your immune cell markers (HLA)—can determine whether your body views a safe pharmaceutical as a dangerous intruder.

vocab.meaning: A super common antibiotic combination used to knock out stubborn bacterial infections like sinus issues.
A condition where bile gets trapped in the liver, turning the skin and the whites of the eyes a striking yellow color.
A mathematical formula doctors use to classify what kind of damage is happening inside a failing liver.
A chemical process where an antibiotic permanently snaps onto an enzyme to shut down bacterial defenses.

quiz.question: When does delayed amoxicillin-clavulanate cholestatic jaundice typically show up?

quiz.question: What does idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury completely throw out the window?

The need for bacterial cell walls to survive

The human body's ability to produce red blood cells
